paragraphs.source_en: Au t hor i t y regarded the principalities surviving beyond 1806 as the primary obstacles to national unification. We need to remove the moral signs, and not simplify the situation as a clash between progressive, proto-democratic fellowship and reactionary lordship. Associational and communal forms were not exclusive to peasants and burghers, but were important to clergy and nobles, as we shall see (pp. 553–​62), while communes could also be lords (pp. 516–​ 18 and 579–​91). Lordship and fellowship did not merely co‑exist but were closely interdependent. Above all, the ideology of the common good, like government techniques, was not simply pioneered by citizens only to be stolen later by princes. Instead, hierarchical and horizontal forms worked in ‘creative tension’,33 producing new ideas and practices.
